df = sns.load_dataset('car_crashes')
df.sample(5)

# Method

Given that we have two columns of continuous data (percentage of alcohol-impaired drivers and car insurance premiums by dollar), we will evaluate this relationship using simple correlation analysis. We will also display the analysis using a scatterplot. 

# Results

```{python}
corr_val = np.array(df[['alcohol', 'ins_premium']].corr())[0][1]

print(corr_val)

narrative = "a very strong negative correlation"
if corr_val > .8: 
    narrative = "a very strong positive correlation"
elif corr_val > .4: 
    narrative = "a moderate positive correlation"
elif corr_val > 0:
    narrative = "a weak positive correlation" 
elif corr_val > -.4:
    narrative = "a weak negative correlation" 
elif corr_val > .8: 
    narrative = "a moderate negative correlation"
```

Using the simple Pearson correlation approach, these data produce a correlation coefficient of `{python} f"{corr_val:.4f}"`; given this result, we conclude that there is `{python} narrative` between rate of alcohol-impaired drivers and cost of car insurance premiums. 

```{python}
#| label: fig-alc-prem-scatterplot 
#| fig-cap: "A scatterplot of alcohol-impaired drivers and insurance premiums"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize = (6, 3.5))
sns.scatterplot(data = df, y = 'ins_premium', x = 'alcohol')

plt.xlabel('Percentage of Alcohol-Impaired Drivers')
plt.ylabel('Car Insurance Premiums ($)')
```

As show in in @fig-alc-prem-scatterplot we see additional evidence of a strong positive correlation between the rate of alcohol-impaired drivers and cost of car insurance premiums.

# Discussion

We have established that there is a weakly negative correlation between rate of alcohol-impaired drivers and insurance premiums. Although correlation is only one statistic, I am going to tell all of my friends that drinking does not increase our premiums and we should keep buying drinks for drinking and driving!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
